answers.displayAnswer: A mechanical wave is an oscillation or disturbance that propagates through an elastic medium. A displaced particle exerts forces on its neighbors, making them oscillate in turn, so the disturbance spreads from place to place. The particles vibrate locally; they do not travel through the medium with the wave.

In a transverse wave, the particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction in which the wave travels. For example, a sideways disturbance travels along a stretched cord while each part of the cord moves across that direction.

In a longitudinal wave, the particles vibrate parallel to the direction in which the wave travels. Pushing and pulling a spring along its length produces traveling compressions and rarefactions. Sound in air is also longitudinal: air particles oscillate back and forth along the direction of sound propagation.

The basic characteristic of wave motion is that the disturbance and energy travel through the medium without sustained bulk transport of its mass. In the ideal mechanical-wave model, each particle oscillates about its own equilibrium position rather than moving along with the wave.

For example, in the ball-and-spring chain, a deformed spring exerts a force and does work on the next ball. Energy passes from ball to ball through the springs, while the balls remain local oscillators. This does not mean that the particles are motionless.

Wavelength $\lambda$ is the distance along the direction of propagation between the nearest distinct points vibrating in the same phase. Such points repeat the same vibration state together, with the same displacement and direction of motion. Equal displacement at just one instant is not sufficient if their directions of motion differ.

Examples are the distance from one crest to the next crest, or from one compression to the next compression. In Figure 70, the separation along the undisturbed chain from ball 1 to ball 13 is one wavelength.

In one vibration period $T$, the wave pattern travels one wavelength $\lambda$. Therefore its propagation speed is $v=\frac{\lambda}{T}=\lambda\nu$, where $\nu=\frac{1}{T}$ is the vibration frequency. Wave speed equals wavelength multiplied by frequency. At a fixed frequency, a larger wavelength corresponds to a larger wave speed. This is the wave's propagation speed, not the instantaneous velocity of a vibrating particle.

In Figure 70e, one wavelength extends from ball 1 to ball 13, covering twelve equal adjacent intervals along the undisturbed chain. The adjacent spacing is therefore $d=\frac{\lambda}{12}$.

For two adjacent balls that have entered the vibration, the phase-difference magnitude is $|\Delta\phi|=\frac{2\pi d}{\lambda}=\frac{\pi}{6}$ radians, or $30^\circ$. Along the direction of propagation, the next ball lags the preceding ball by one twelfth of a cycle, corresponding to a time delay $\frac{T}{12}$. The $\frac{T}{4}$ interval between successive panels is not the delay between adjacent balls.
